heading: Sample 2
content:
Let me explain my roles and responsibilities.

Every day, when I start my shift, the first thing I do is review the
previous shift's handover email to understand the current status of the
application and any ongoing issues.

Similarly, before I log out, I prepare and send a handover email to the
next shift with all the important updates.

We also have a daily catch-up call with my team. In that call, we
discuss things like:

- What tickets are currently open.

- Which tickets are still pending.

- Which tickets have been escalated and need immediate attention.

- Which tickets are dependent on other IT teams.

If we come across any new issue that has been resolved, we share the
knowledge with the team, explaining how the issue was identified and
resolved so that everyone can handle similar issues in the future.

These are the kinds of topics we usually discuss during our daily team
call.

Apart from that, one of my key responsibilities is prioritizing
incidents based on the SLA. I make sure to respond to and resolve the
incidents assigned to my ticket queue within the agreed timelines.

So, that's it about me and thank you for giving this opportunity to
Introduce myself.

Tell Your Incident Flow

• So usually, the incident Is raised by the end user or service desk
team.

•Once I get an incident, I will first check if the incident belongs to
my queue or not, If the Incident does not belong to my queue, I will
reroute the incident to the correct team or I will reroute the incident
to the service desk (Service Desk team has a catalogue which team has to
take of which incident).

• Now, once I know the ticket belongs to my queue, I check if I have all
the information, I need to resolve it. If something's missing, I reach
out to the user directly chat with them on Teams or through ServiceNow
and gather whatever I need, like what URL they were using, when they
faced the issue, what time, what browser, and so on.

• Then I will respond to the Ticket based on sla

We follow SLA in our company

We have response time and resolution time

1\. Response Time

How soon you should give a response to the Incident

2.Resolution time

How soon you should resolve the Incident

For example:

if the customer application or a functionality

is not working multiple team we consider that p1 issue,

we should response within 10 minutes and resolution time is 2 hours

if the customer application or a functionality

is not working multiple users we consider that p2 issue,

we should response within 45 minutes and resolution time is 4 hours.

After that, I try to recreate or reproduce the issue myself. If it's
working fine on my end, I take a remote connection with the user and try
to see what's going wrong specifically at their end.

If it's not working, I check our KEDB document --- that's our
knowledge base, it has issues and resolutions for everything we've
faced before. I follow the steps mentioned there and resolve it.

If it's a completely new issue that's not in the KEDB, I troubleshoot
it myself and then add it into the KEDB, so the next time someone hits
the same issue, they can just refer to the document and fix it. I'd say
the KEDB is basically like the Wikipedia of our company.

Once the issue is resolved, I attach a screenshot, mark it resolved in
ServiceNow, and send an email to the user letting them know it's been
fixed.
